day1.text: Hello, commander, I'm Lira from Mission Control! Today, April 17, 2024, the Sun flared (class M1.6) and threw out a cloud of plasma that is flying toward us.
day1.lesson: A plasma cloud from the Sun (CME) takes a few days to reach the Moon, so we have time to get ready.

day2.text: On April 18 the Sun is restless again: a class M2.2 flare and two more plasma clouds heading our way. They will arrive together with yesterday's cloud on April 21.
day2.lesson: Flares come in classes A, B, C, M and X, and each class is 10 times stronger than the one before.

day3.text: On April 19 there is a class M2.1 flare on the Sun. And on Earth today there is a strong magnetic storm, so people in the north can see the northern lights!
day3.lesson: Earth's magnetic field protects it from solar particles, but the Moon has no such shield.

day4.text: April 20 is a quiet day: the strongest flare is just a tiny C3.9. A great time to charge the batteries and do some science!
day4.lesson: Even on a quiet day there is weak cosmic radiation on the Moon, because there is no air here to stop it.

day5.text: On April 21 the plasma clouds that left on April 17 and 18 have reached the Moon! Plus an M3.4 flare, so it's time to think about the shelter.
day5.lesson: The plasma cloud flew 150 million kilometers from the Sun in about 4 days.

day6.text: On April 22 there are four M-class flares on the Sun, and the strongest is M2.8. The Sun is warming up!
day6.lesson: Flares explode in sunspots: dark areas where the Sun's magnetic field is tangled.

day7.text: April 23 brings an M3.6 flare and three new plasma clouds flying toward us. Today is the last day of week one, so check your battery and life support!
day7.lesson: NASA scientists watch the Sun with space telescopes and calculate when a plasma cloud will arrive.

day8.text: April 24 brings an M2.0 flare and one more plasma cloud heading our way. It will catch up with yesterday's clouds, and they will all arrive on April 26.
day8.lesson: Plasma clouds fly at different speeds: a fast one can catch up with a slow one that left earlier.

day9.text: On April 25 the Sun is a bit calmer: just an M1.3 flare. The plasma clouds are still on their way and will arrive in one day.
day9.lesson: Light from a flare reaches the Moon in about 8 minutes, but a plasma cloud takes a few days.

day10.text: On April 26 the plasma clouds that left on April 23 and 24 have hit the Moon! Good thing we knew about them in advance.
day10.lesson: One plasma cloud can weigh a billion tons: a whole mountain of super-hot gas.

day11.text: On April 27 there is a class M3.0 flare on the Sun. The Sun is shining bright, and the batteries are charging well.
day11.lesson: A lunar day lasts about 14 Earth days, and the whole time the solar panels make energy.

day12.text: April 28 is the quietest day of the week, with no strong flares at all. Perfect for science!
day12.lesson: The Moon's surface is covered with regolith, a layer of fine dust and pebbles that can shield a base from radiation.

day13.text: On April 29 there is an M3.7 flare on the Sun. The Sun is slowly sinking toward the horizon: the lunar night is coming.
day13.lesson: The Moon always shows the same side to Earth, so from the base Earth stays in the same spot in the sky.

day14.text: April 30 brings an M9.5 flare, almost class X! This is the last sunny day before the long night, so charge the batteries as much as you can.
day14.lesson: An M9.5 flare is only a little weaker than X1, because the border between classes is very close.

day15.text: On May 1 the lunar night has come to the base, and the Sun has gone below the horizon. Energy is low now, so spend your tokens carefully.
day15.lesson: A lunar night lasts about 14 Earth days, and the cold drops to −173 °C.

day16.text: On May 2 there is an M2.7 flare on the Sun and a magnetic storm on Earth. It's dark here, but Mission Control sends you Sun news every day.
day16.lesson: Solar particles fly along curved magnetic lines, so they can reach the base even at night.

day17.text: May 3 brings the first X-class flare of the mission, X1.6, and three plasma clouds heading our way! Radio contact may be lost tomorrow, so remember: the clouds will arrive on May 6.
day17.lesson: An X-class flare disturbs radio contact, because its light stirs up the upper layer of Earth's atmosphere.

day18.text: On May 4 the radio link with Earth is noisy after yesterday's X flare, and there is no forecast. Meanwhile the Sun has fired off an M9.1 flare.
day18.lesson: The ionosphere is a layer of air high above Earth that radio signals travel through, and flares "blind" it.

day19.text: On May 5 there are two X-class flares at once: X1.3 and X1.2! Radio contact may be lost again tomorrow.
day19.lesson: A big group of sunspots can flare many times in a row while it faces us.

day20.text: On May 6 the plasma clouds we learned about on May 3 have reached the Moon, plus an X4.5 flare! There is no radio contact, so remember what Lira warned you about.
day20.lesson: An X4.5 flare is about 4.5 times stronger than an X1 flare.

day21.text: May 7 brings an M8.2 flare and two big plasma clouds flying straight at us. They will arrive on May 10, so get the shelter ready in advance!
day21.lesson: A giant group of sunspots called AR 3664 has grown on the Sun: about 15 times wider than Earth.

day22.text: On May 8 there are two X1.0 flares from the same giant sunspot. Radio contact may be lost tomorrow, and the plasma clouds are already on their way.
day22.lesson: The Sun's activity rises and falls in a cycle of about 11 years, and 2024 is close to the peak.

day23.text: On May 9 a radiation storm has begun: the Sun has sped up particles to nearly the speed of light! Plus X2.2 and X1.1 flares, and there is no radio contact with Earth.
day23.lesson: Radiation storm particles fly from the Sun in tens of minutes and pass through thin walls.

day24.text: On May 10 the plasma clouds hit Earth and the Moon: the strongest magnetic storm in more than 20 years! The radiation storm goes on, and the Sun added an X3.9 flare.
day24.lesson: That night people saw the northern lights even in Ukraine, because Earth is protected by its magnetic field, but the Moon has none.

day25.text: On May 11 the Sun exploded with an X5.8 flare, the strongest of the whole mission so far! The radiation storm is not calming down, so keep your crew safe.
day25.lesson: The best protection from radiation is a thick layer of regolith or water between the astronauts and space.

day26.text: On May 12 there is an X1.0 flare on the Sun, and the magnetic storm is still echoing on Earth. Radio contact may be lost tomorrow.
day26.lesson: During a magnetic storm, scientists keep an eye on satellites and power grids, because solar particles can damage them.

day27.text: May 13 brings a new radiation storm and an M6.6 flare, and there is no radio contact with Earth. Hang in there, sunrise is very close!
day27.lesson: Astronauts wear dosimeters: devices that count how much radiation they have received.

day28.text: May 14 brings an X8.7 flare, the strongest since 2017! Its plasma cloud will arrive only after we leave, and tomorrow is sunrise.
day28.lesson: The Sun turns around once in about a month, so the giant sunspot is moving past the edge and firing past us.

day29.text: May 15 is sunrise, and the Sun is back over the base, bringing X3.4 and X2.9 flares! Today give tokens to prepare the rocket, because we leave tomorrow.
day29.lesson: It is easier for a rocket to take off from the Moon than from Earth, because gravity here is 6 times weaker.

day30.text: May 16 is departure day, and the Sun is finally calm: just an M1.0 flare. You've made it through 30 days of real space weather, and Mission Control is proud of you, commander!
day30.lesson: All 30 days of the game are real events from NASA's DONKI database, recorded in April and May 2024.
